# MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training

Xiangyu Peng    Jiaxin Zhang    An Yan    Yu Li Affiliation: Ran Xu,
Zeyuan Chen, Chien-Sheng Wu Email: [becky.peng@salesforce.com](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong visual
reasoners, yet remain limited in open-world, multi-step search that
requires grounding images, selecting tools, and integrating web
evidence. Existing approaches typically construct and filter fixed
offline corpora whose question distributions cannot adapt as the target
deep-search agent improves. Building on MTA-Agent’s image-grounded QA
construction ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)), we present MTA-Zero, an
online multimodal QA–Solver co-training framework for self-improving
multimodal deep-search agents that requires no precomputed multi-hop
corpus. Starting from image-grounded VQA seed contexts, a trainable QA
Generator retrieves evidence and constructs verified multi-hop questions
online. A separate deep-search Solver then selects tools, gathers
evidence, and answers the generated questions. To focus generation on
the Solver’s learning frontier, we derive a Goldilocks reward for the QA
Generator from the Solver’s group-wise rollout success rate: questions
solved by all rollouts or by none receive zero reward, whereas questions
near the current frontier are favored. We optimize the two policies
independently with GRPO, without sharing parameters or gradients. Across
six multimodal deep-search benchmarks, MTA-Zero improves a Qwen3-VL-8B
Solver from $`36.91\%`$ to $`51.58\%`$ mean accuracy and achieves
performance comparable to GPT-5 under the same agent workflow. The same
framework also improves a newer Qwen3.6-27B Solver by $`10.82`$ points.
These results show that verified online question generation provides a
policy-specific curriculum for continually improving multimodal
deep-search agents.

## 1 Introduction

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress
in visual understanding and reasoning ([Xue et al., 2024](#bib.bib22);
[DeepSeek-AI, 2025](#bib.bib23); [Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib24);
[Qwen-Team, 2025](#bib.bib25)). Yet, turning them into open-world agents
that can identify entities in images, gather web evidence, and compose
multi-hop answers through external tools remains challenging ([Geng et
al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Chng et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib28)). Improving a target multimodal deep-search agent
remains an open problem. We refer to this deployment-time agent as the
_Solver agent_. The Solver must learn not only to reason over an image,
but also to decide what to search for, which tools to invoke, and how to
integrate evidence collected across modalities.

A dominant approach is to improve multimodal deep-search agents through
an offline data factory ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib1); [Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib7); [Yao et al., 2026](#bib.bib6); [Chen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib5)). Starting from seed images or questions, capable
models and tools synthesize candidate multi-hop QA pairs and search
trajectories; verification and filtering then turn them into SFT or RL
corpora such as MTA-Agent ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)),
MM-DeepResearch ([Yao et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)), and REDSearcher ([Chu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)). These pipelines create valuable, broadly
reusable datasets, but their question distributions are fixed before the
target Solver begins to evolve. As the Solver evolves, a generic
question may be unanswerable at an early stage, trivial at a later one,
or simply unrelated to its current capability gaps. Consequently, a
fixed offline corpus may devote much of its generation, verification,
and tool-interaction workload to questions that are no longer
informative for the evolving policy.

This mismatch suggests an alternative: allowing training questions to
evolve with the Solver itself. Self-improvement and Generator–Solver
co-evolution have shown that adaptive task generation can create
curricula that track an agent’s changing capabilities, in both
text-based search and vision-language reasoning ([Lu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib8); [Yue et al., 2026](#bib.bib9); [He et al.,
2025](#bib.bib14); [Thawakar et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)). However, this idea is substantially harder in
multimodal deep search. A useful question must be grounded in the seed
image, supported by external evidence, answerable through an independent
multi-hop tool trajectory, and free of ambiguous answers or evidence
leakage. Moreover, optimizing a QA Generator only for Solver failures
encourages unanswerable questions, whereas optimizing only for success
collapses the curriculum to trivial ones. The challenge is therefore to
train a QA Generator that produces verified questions at the evolving
Solver’s learning frontier.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
previews this curriculum mismatch and the effect of adapting the QA
policy online.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: Why co-training the QA policy matters. Left: a frozen but
valid QA policy produces progressively fewer informative questions as
the Solver improves: the fraction of held-out QA groups with
non-degenerate rollout outcomes ($`0<p_{i}<1`$) falls from $`55.8\%`$ at
$`S_{0}`$ to $`44.3\%`$ at $`S_{50}`$. When the QA policy is updated
online alongside the Solver, matched checkpoints retain or restore this
training signal. Right: per-benchmark accuracy for selected $`8`$B
agents on MMSrch-Plus, BC-VL, MMSrch, and FVQA. MTA-Zero is highlighted
in teal; the MMSrch bar includes the stronger reported specialist
baseline. Missing bars denote benchmarks not reported by the
corresponding prior work.

We address this challenge with MTA-Zero, which adapts MTA-Agent’s
verified QA-construction pipeline ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)) for
asymmetric online co-training of two separate models: a QA Generator and
a Solver. The QA Generator is trained to produce appropriately
challenging questions for the Solver, while the Solver is trained to
answer multimodal deep-search questions. Given a seed image and QA pair,
the QA Generator proposes multi-hop multimodal deep search QA pairs, and
the Solver receives only the image and final question, then produces
multiple independent tool-use rollouts. For each generated question, the
fraction of correct Solver rollouts determines both learning signals:
the QA Generator is rewarded for mixed outcomes, which indicate
questions that are challenging but solvable, while the Solver is updated
with GRPO on the same rollout groups. As the Solver improves, its
rollout feedback trains the QA Generator to target the Solver’s
remaining capability gaps. The two models use separate parameters,
optimizers, and gradient updates.

Contributions. We propose MTA-Zero, an asymmetric online QA–Solver
co-training framework that updates both a multimodal deep-search QA
Generator and a Solver online. The QA Generator is trained from Solver
rollout feedback to generate appropriately challenging questions, while
the Solver is trained on the resulting question groups with mixed
rollout outcomes. MTA-Zero improves an $`8`$B Solver from $`36.91\%`$ to
$`51.58\%`$ mean accuracy across six evaluation benchmarks,
outperforming the compared $`7`$–$`8`$B specialist agents on four of six
benchmarks and approaching GPT-$`5`$ agent performance with an $`8`$B
model. The same pipeline also transfers to a newer $`27`$B backbone. It
requires no human intervention or manual filtering, no pre-generated
multi-hop corpus, and no additional task-specific SFT stage.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Multimodal Deep Search and Data Construction

Multimodal deep-search agents combine visual reasoning with external
tools such as text and image search, browsing, and OCR ([Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib28); [Narayan et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Geng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2); [Chng et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)). Their long-horizon
supervision is commonly prepared offline. A typical pipeline first
selects seed images or questions, uses capable models and tools to
synthesize candidate multi-hop questions, answers, and search
trajectories, then verifies evidence support and filters invalid,
ambiguous, duplicate, or shortcut-prone examples before assembling SFT
or RL corpora. MTA-Agent ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)),
DeepMMSearch-R1 ([Narayan et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)), VSearcher ([Zhang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)), MM-DeepResearch ([Yao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6)), and OpenSearch-VL ([Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib5))
instantiate variants of this recipe with tool-assisted generation and
quality, difficulty, or trajectory filtering. REDSearcher ([Chu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20)) and HyperEyes ([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib21)) further
combine such offline curation with controllable task complexity and
efficiency-oriented trajectory selection, respectively. ODE ([Huang et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib4)) makes the pipeline more policy-aware through
on-policy data evolution. In contrast, we jointly train an
image-grounded QA generator and a multi-tool Solver online. The Solver’s
group-wise success rate provides a Goldilocks signal that updates the QA
generator; as the Solver improves, the generator learns to pose new
questions at its shifting learning frontier, and the Solver is in turn
trained on these online-generated questions. Unlike a fixed, potentially
stronger offline generator that prepares a broadly useful corpus for
many downstream models, our QA generator is optimized against the
current Solver and can focus on questions that expose its specific
capability gaps. Thus, the training distribution adapts online rather
than being fixed in a pre-generated multi-hop corpus.

### 2.2 Self-Improving and Co-Evolution

In text-based search, Search Self-play ([Lu et al., 2026](#bib.bib8))
and Dr. Zero ([Yue et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)) co-evolve task proposal and
solving to create an adaptive curriculum. R-Zero ([Huang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib10)), Absolute Zero ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)),
Tool-R0 ([Acikgoz et al., 2026](#bib.bib12)), and Agent0 ([Xia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13)) extend this principle to reasoning and general
tool-use environments. For vision-language models, VisPlay ([He et al.,
2025](#bib.bib14)), EvoLMM ([Thawakar et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)), and
V-Zero ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)) use Questioner–Solver loops
over visual inputs, while Vision-Zero ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)),
iReasoner ([Sunil et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)), and Agent0-VL ([Liu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib17)) explore strategic self-play, intrinsic rewards,
or tool-grounded self-refinement. Our setting instead targets open-world
multimodal deep search. Although MTA-Zero follows the same
co-evolutionary intuition, multimodal deep search poses a substantially
harder task-generation problem: the QA Generator must retrieve and
verify external evidence, preserve visual grounding and entity
continuity across multiple hops, and calibrate question difficulty for
an independently acting Solver that uses heterogeneous tools. A question
that appears plausible from an image may still be unanswerable,
ambiguous, or unsupported by the retrieved evidence, making naive task
proposal unreliable. MTA-Zero therefore combines a fixed verification
harness with Solver-calibrated rewards to construct a reliable,
capability-adaptive curriculum.

## 3 Method

As
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
shows, MTA-Zero co-trains a training-time QA Generator
$`\pi_{\mathrm{Q}}`$ and a target multimodal deep-search Solver
$`\pi_{\mathrm{S}}`$. At iteration $`t`$, we start from an
image-grounded seed context $`C=(I,q^{1},a^{1})`$. The QA generator
$`\pi_{\mathrm{Q}}^{t}`$
(§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Online QA Generation with a Harness ‣ 3 Method ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training"))
produces $`N_{\mathrm{QA}}`$ evidence-grounded candidate QA pairs
$`\{(I,q_{i},a_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{QA}}}`$. For every accepted
$`q_{i}`$, the Solver $`\pi_{\mathrm{S}}^{t}`$
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Multi-tool Solver Rollouts ‣ 3 Method ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training"))
receives $`(I,q_{i})`$ and makes $`K`$ independent multi-step tool-use
rollouts. Let $`p_{i}`$ be the fraction of those attempts whose final
answers are correct. This one scalar closes the loop in two distinct
ways. First, we map $`p_{i}`$ to a Goldilocks reward
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Solver-Calibrated QA Scores ‣ 3 Method ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training"))
for the QA trajectory that proposed $`q_{i}`$: questions solved by all
rollouts or by none receive no QA reward, while questions near the
target success rate are preferred. Second, the $`K`$ attempts form one
Solver GRPO group. The QA generator receives only this scalar-derived
reward; the Solver is updated from its own individual rollout outcomes.
No gradient is passed between the two policies, which retain separate
parameters and optimizers.

![Refer to caption](2610.33799v1/mds-zero-paper.png)

Figure 2: Overview of MTA-Zero. The QA Generator and Solver are updated
online from separate GRPO objectives, while the fixed harness executes
and validates QA-construction actions. The QA-side tool palette depicts
the general harness interface; the main experiments enable web-text
search only for QA construction.

### 3.1 Online QA Generation with a Harness

The QA Generator is a trainable agent that constructs challenging
multi-hop multimodal QA pairs for training the deep-search Solver agent.
It includes: ($`1`$) a trainable LLM policy that writes web-search
queries, then proposes a single-hop question–answer pair grounded in the
retrieved evidence; and ($`2`$) a fixed, non-trainable harness that
executes the policy’s actions, checks the validity of each proposed hop,
and merges accepted single-hop QA pairs into a final multi-hop QA task.

Growing an $`n`$-hop question. Rather than precomputing a generic
training corpus, the QA Generator $`\pi_{\mathrm{Q}}`$ converts a seed
context $`C=(I,q^{1},a^{1})`$ into a multi-hop QA pair online. We count
$`C`$ as the first of $`n`$ hops and set $`\bar{q}^{1}:=q^{1}`$; its
answer $`a^{1}`$ is the initial entity to explore. For each subsequent
hop $`h\in\{2,\ldots,n\}`$, $`\pi_{\mathrm{Q}}`$ searches for
information about the previous answer $`a^{h-1}`$, then proposes an
evidence-based QA pair $`(q^{h},a^{h})`$. The new question $`q^{h}`$
asks for a fact about the previous entity $`a^{h-1}`$, while its answer
$`a^{h}`$ identifies the entity used to extend the next hop. For each
non-final hop, this entity must be specific, and evidence-supported
(Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Bridge-Entity Definition and Generator State ‣ Appendix A Detailed Agent Protocols ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")).
Once the proposal is accepted, the harness combines $`q^{h}`$ with the
running question $`\bar{q}^{h-1}`$ to produce $`\bar{q}^{h}`$.
Crucially, this merge removes the explicit mention of $`a^{h-1}`$: the
resulting question reaches $`a^{h}`$ through the preceding description
rather than revealing the intermediate answer. Repeating this process to
the target depth $`n`$ yields $`(I,q_{i},a_{i})=(I,\bar{q}^{n},a^{n})`$.
An example is illustrated in
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 A Recorded QA Generation Trajectory ‣ Appendix A Detailed Agent Protocols ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").

Learned LLM policy. The learned policy selects the next action and
writes that action’s arguments. It alternates between ($`1`$) a
web-search action containing a query and ($`2`$) a propose-next-hop
action containing a candidate question, answer, supporting evidence, and
a source field. Thus, the policy learns both what information to seek
and how to turn that information into the next QA hop.

Non-trainable QA harness. Our fixed harness adapts the offline
verification-and-merging pipeline of MTA-Agent ([Peng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib1)) for online policy training. After a search action, it
retrieves pages, filters them into bounded evidence chunks, and returns
those chunks as an observation for the subsequent proposal action. After
a proposed hop, it checks that the question is anchored to, and actually
requires, the current entity. It then checks the answer uniqueness,
temporal stability, and self-contained wording. It rejects
source-referential, vague, generic, or otherwise non-chainable
proposals. Finally, the harness merges an accepted proposal with the
running question, verifies that the merged question uniquely resolves to
the intended answer, and discards questions that a fixed direct-answer
check can solve without search. More details can be found in the
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B QA Harness Checks and Feedback ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").

Harness feedback and accepted-hop training. For every proposed hop, the
harness appends a feedback message to the context as a user turn. When a
hop is accepted, this message contains the updated merged question
$`\bar{q}^{h}`$, the next entity $`a^{h}`$, and the acceptance signal;
the QA Generator then uses this updated context to select its next
action. Only action trajectories that lead to an accepted hop are used
to train $`\pi_{\mathrm{Q}}`$. If a proposal is rejected, its retrieved
evidence and proposed hop are retained only as context and diagnostic
feedback for a new attempt; all policy tokens associated with that
unsuccessful attempt are masked from the training loss. Representative
feedback and token-level credit assignment are provided in
Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Recorded Harness Feedback ‣ Appendix B QA Harness Checks and Feedback ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
and
Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Learning Boundary of the Fixed Harness ‣ Appendix B QA Harness Checks and Feedback ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training"),
respectively.

### 3.2 Multi-tool Solver Rollouts

For each accepted training question $`q_{i}`$, we sample $`K`$
independent ReAct rollouts. At step $`t`$ of rollout $`j`$, the Solver
either selects a tool and generates its arguments or terminates by
producing a final answer. When a tool is selected, the environment
executes the call and appends the returned observation to the history,
yielding $`H_{ij}^{t+1}`$ for the next decision. This interaction loop
continues until the Solver returns a final answer or reaches the maximum
number of interaction steps. Let $`c_{ij}\in\{0,1\}`$ denote the
terminal correctness of rollout $`j`$ for question $`q_{i}`$, determined
by answer matching
(Appendix [D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 Answer Scoring and LLM Adjudication ‣ Appendix D Training and Evaluation Details ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")).
The group success rate is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       p_{i}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}c_{ij}.
       ```                                     |     | (1) |

We update $`\pi_{\mathrm{S}}`$ with standard GRPO only when
$`0<p_{i}<1`$. These groups contain both correct and incorrect rollouts
and therefore provide a useful relative learning signal.

### 3.3 Solver-Calibrated QA Scores

The same rate $`p_{i}`$ supplies an adaptive difficulty signal for the
QA generator. We map it to a Goldilocks score,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       r^{\mathrm{Q}}_{i}=\begin{cases}0,&p_{i}\in\{0,1\},\\
       \dfrac{p_{i}}{\tau},&0<p_{i}\leq\tau,\\
       \dfrac{1-p_{i}}{1-\tau},&\tau<p_{i}<1,\end{cases}
       ```                                                    |     | (2) |

where $`\tau\in(0,1)`$ is the target Solver success rate. The reward
peaks at $`p_{i}=\tau`$, while questions solved by every rollout or by
none receive zero reward. Optimizing $`\pi_{\mathrm{Q}}`$ with GRPO
therefore favors questions that are difficult but still solvable by the
current Solver, rather than questions that merely maximize failure. For
clarity, our main setting uses $`K=8`$ and $`\tau=0.5`$. Thus, when
$`k=0,\ldots,8`$ of the eight Solver rollouts answer a question
correctly, its QA score is

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\begin{array}[]{c|ccccccccc}k&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\
\hline\cr r_{i}^{\mathrm{Q}}&0&.25&.50&.75&1.00&.75&.50&.25&0\end{array}.
``` |  |

Every QA candidate is scored separately. For one seed, the figure’s
$`N_{\mathrm{QA}}=8`$ candidates yield the reward set
$`\{r_{i}^{\mathrm{Q}}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{QA}}}`$, which is used to
optimize $`\pi_{\mathrm{Q}}`$ with GRPO over these QA-generation
trajectories. This per-candidate assignment is what allows the
curriculum to track the Solver’s changing learning frontier.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experiment Setup

#### 4.1.1 Datasets

Evaluation. We evaluate the trained Solver on six benchmarks that
require visual evidence understanding and open-web research:
MMSearch-Plus (MMSrch-Plus) ([Tao et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)),
HR-MMSearch-VL (HR-MMSrch) ([Chng et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)),
BrowseComp-VL (BC-VL) ([Geng et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)), MMSearch-VL
(MMSrch) ([Jiang et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)), the testmini split of
VDR-Bench (VDR) ([Huang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib30)), and the official
FVQA test split (FVQA) ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)).

Training seeds. Following the publicly described seed-source protocol of
MTA-Agent ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)), we initialize co-training
from a fixed image-grounded one-hop VQA pool: InfoSeek ([Chen et al.,
2023](#bib.bib35)), the training split of FVQA ([Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib28)), InfoVQA ([Mathew et al., 2022](#bib.bib37)), and
OK-VQA ([Marino et al., 2019](#bib.bib36)). Each seed contains only
$`C=(I,q^{1},a^{1})`$: an image, its original one-hop question, and its
answer.
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Seed-Pool Construction ‣ Appendix D Training and Evaluation Details ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
gives the exact pool composition and filtering rules. The pool provides
initial visual grounding rather than an offline deep-search corpus: it
contains no pre-generated multi-hop QA pairs, retrieved evidence, or
search trajectories. All multi-hop questions used for optimization are
subsequently constructed and verified online by the QA generator and
harness in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Online QA Generation with a Harness ‣ 3 Method ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").

#### 4.1.2 Agent Setup

Solver Setup. We use a ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) framework ([Yao et
al., 2022](#bib.bib32)) for the deep-search Solver
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Multi-tool Solver Rollouts ‣ 3 Method ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")).
It operates for at most $`T=10`$ iterations. At each iteration, it
generates a structured output comprising (i) a reasoning trace based on
the current state, (ii) an action specifying a tool and its parameters,
(iii) a binary should_stop flag, and (iv) a scalar confidence score. The
loop terminates early when should_stop=true and the confidence score
exceeds $`0.7`$, or the maximum budget of $`T=10`$ iterations is
exhausted. Upon termination, the agent generates its final answer
conditioned on the complete interaction history. Further details are
provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Solver Interaction and Tool Interfaces ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").

QA Agent setup. The QA Generator follows the construction-specific
interaction loop described in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Online QA Generation with a Harness ‣ 3 Method ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").
For each seed context, we sample $`8`$ QA-generation trajectories with
max_turns set to $`16`$. At a search step, the Generator emits action,
thought, tool, and query; the harness executes web-text search, filters
the returned pages into evidence chunks, and appends them to the next
interaction state. At a proposal step, it emits action, thought,
question, answer, evidence, and source. The harness verifies the
proposal and, if accepted, appends the merged question and next entity;
otherwise, it returns diagnostic feedback. A trajectory terminates after
reaching the target depth or exhausting its configured turn budget.
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Bridge-Entity Definition and Generator State ‣ Appendix A Detailed Agent Protocols ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
specifies the state and action schemas.

Tool Palette. The Solver has access to: Web search retrieves web
results, including snippets, titles, and URLs. Image search returns
textual descriptions of images found on the web. Web URL reader extracts
the full text of a given webpage. Reverse image search uses Google Lens
to identify objects and landmarks. OCR extracts visible text from an
image, and image cropping extracts a specified region from an image. All
Solver tool calls are sent to a local observation server, and the
returned observation is appended to the chat history for the next
action. More details are in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Tool Palette ‣ Appendix C Solver Interaction and Tool Interfaces ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").

#### 4.1.3 Baselines

We compare to three commercial large language models: GPT-$`5`$ ([Singh
et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)), Claude Sonnet $`4.5`$, and Gemini $`3`$
Pro ([DeepMind, 2025](#bib.bib34)). We evaluate each model under two
settings: ($`1`$) direct answering without tools and ($`2`$) agent-based
answering using the same framework and tool configuration as our method.
In addition, we report results from prior work: MTA-DeepSearch ([Peng et
al., 2026](#bib.bib1)), MMSearch-R1 ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)),
SenseNova-MARS ([Chng et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)), WebWatcher ([Geng et
al., 2025](#bib.bib26)), VSearcher ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)),
MM-DeepResearch ([Yao et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)), OpenSearch-VL ([Chen et
al., 2026](#bib.bib5)), ODE ([Huang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib4)), and
Vision-DeepResearch.

#### 4.1.4 Training Setup

The QA generator and Solver begin from separate copies of
Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct ([Qwen-Team, 2025](#bib.bib25)). Instead of
synthesizing a multi-hop corpus before training, we initialize online
generation from a fixed pool of image-grounded, one-hop VQA seed
contexts in
Section [4.1.1](#S4.SS1.SSS1 "4.1.1 Datasets ‣ 4.1 Experiment Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").
Each optimization iteration draws $`8`$ seed QAs from the pool. The QA
policy generates $`8`$ trajectories targeting a total depth of $`5`$
hops (one seed hop and four extensions) per seed, and every retained QA
is answered by $`8`$ independently sampled Solver rollouts. This
produces $`64`$ QA trajectories and $`512=8\times 8\times 8`$ Solver
trajectories in one iteration. We optimize the two policies
independently with GRPO for $`50`$ iterations, with learning rate
$`10^{-6}`$, and Goldilocks target $`\tau=0.5`$. The QA generator and
Solver have turn caps of $`16`$ and $`10`$; their prompt and response
limits are $`8,192`$ and $`24,576`$ tokens, respectively. All main
$`8`$B numbers come from the Solver after the $`50`$th co-training
iteration. Full configuration is in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Training and Evaluation Details ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
and online data and resource accounting are in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Online Data and Workload Accounting ‣ Appendix D Training and Evaluation Details ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").

### 4.2 Main Results

Strong improvement without a pre-generated multi-hop corpus. As shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training"),
comparing to the matched Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct Agent Workflow baseline
(in gray), MTA-Zero raises the six benchmark mean accuracy from
$`36.91\%`$ to $`51.58\%`$ ($`+14.67`$ points). The run uses $`400`$
one-hop seed-context draws over $`50`$ co-training iterations: the QA
generator and Solver are optimized directly with GRPO, without a
separate multi-hop data factory or an additional task-specific SFT
stage. Full resource and service-use accounting is reported in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Online Data and Workload Accounting ‣ Appendix D Training and Evaluation Details ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").

Comparison with $`7`$–$`8`$B specialist deep-search agents. Among the
specialist agents listed in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training"),
MTA-Zero records the highest score on four of six benchmarks. Prior
specialist agents including MTA-Agent ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)),
VSearcher ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)), and OpenSearch-VL ([Chen et
al., 2026](#bib.bib5)) first construct, filter, or reuse offline
teacher-assisted QA or trajectory corpora before applying SFT and/or RL.
Because their results use their original tool stacks and training
pipelines, this is not a cost-matched comparison. However, MTA-Zero and
MTA-DeepSearch ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)) share the same raw
one-hop seed pool: MTA-Zero replaces MTA-DeepSearch’s offline multi-hop
data-construction pipeline with online QA–Solver co-training. Without
pre-generating a multi-hop corpus or adding an additional task-specific
SFT stage, MTA-Zero outperforms MTA-DeepSearch on four of the five
benchmarks for which both methods report results.

Approaching GPT-5 at the 8B scale. Despite using an $`8`$B open model,
MTA-Zero reaches $`51.58\%`$ average accuracy across six benchmarks,
coming within $`0.40`$ percentage points of GPT-$`5`$ under the same
Agent Workflow ($`51.98\%`$). Although stronger commercial agents remain
ahead overall, this result shows that online QA–Solver co-training can
make a compact model competitive with a strong frontier system without
increasing the Solver backbone size.

## 5 Analysis

### 5.1 Does the QA Agent Learn an Adaptive Curriculum?

Before online co-training, the pretrained base model and our fixed QA
harness already function as a QA agent: they can search evidence,
propose next-hop QA pairs, and generate verified multi-hop questions.
The key question is whether further training of this agent is necessary.
We use checkpoint cross-play to assess it. Starting from $`128`$
held-out seed QA pairs, the agent generates $`4`$ questions $`q_{i}`$
per seed. For each generated question, we estimate the Solver’s success
rate $`p_{i}`$ using $`8`$ independent rollouts. We define the
*informative group rate* (I.G. rate) as the proportion of questions with
$`0<p_{i}<1`$, because only these questions yield non-degenerate GRPO
groups for the Solver.

The left panel of
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
tests whether the initial QA agent, $`Q_{0}`$ (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct),
remains suitable as the Solver evolves. Its dashed red curve fixes
$`Q_{0}`$ and varies the Solver from $`S_{0}`$ to $`S_{50}`$. The I.G.
rate falls from $`55.8\%`$ to $`44.3\%`$. Thus, even a capable frozen QA
agent and fixed harness become mismatched to a stronger Solver. We then
fix the Solver at $`S_{50}`$ and use successive QA checkpoints to
generate $`4`$ questions from each of the same $`128`$ held-out seed QA
pairs ($`512`$ questions in total). The right panel of
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Does the QA Agent Learn an Adaptive Curriculum? ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
shows that the I.G. rate rises from $`44.3\%`$ for $`Q_{0}`$ to
$`56.8\%`$ for $`Q_{50}`$, a gain of $`12.5`$ percentage points. Since
the Solver, seed contexts, and fixed harness are unchanged, this gain
comes from the learned QA policy.

The left plot of
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Does the QA Agent Learn an Adaptive Curriculum? ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
reveals how the distribution changes. Relative to $`Q_{0}`$, $`Q_{50}`$
reduces universally failed groups ($`p_{i}=0`$) from $`27.5\%`$ to
$`18.6\%`$ and universally solved groups ($`p_{i}=1`$) from $`28.1\%`$
to $`24.6\%`$. At the same time, it raises the proportion of groups in
the central $`3/8`$–$`5/8`$ success-rate range from $`16.6\%`$ to
$`24.6\%`$. The solid teal curve in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
shows the complementary matched-checkpoint view: its I.G. rate stays
between $`50.1\%`$ and $`56.8\%`$ throughout co-training. Together,
these results show that the QA policy learns to generate questions that
remain useful for the current Solver, rather than supplying a static
distribution that is useful only near initialization.

### 5.2 Ablating the QA Difficulty Target

The Goldilocks reward does not merely reject degenerate question groups:
its target $`\tau`$ specifies the Solver success rate that the QA policy
is encouraged to produce. Our default $`\tau=0.5`$ assigns maximal
reward to questions answered correctly by $`4`$ of $`8`$ Solver
rollouts. We also evaluate a more aggressive low-success target
motivated by Absolute Zero ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)). Its
inverse-accuracy reward is largest when exactly $`1`$ of $`8`$ Solver
rollouts is correct. Rather than directly use such a strict target, we
set $`\tau=0.25`$, which peaks at $`2/8`$ correct rollouts. A lone
correct rollout can be a lucky sample rather than reliable evidence that
the generated question is solvable, whereas $`2`$ correct rollouts
provide a more robust indication of a difficult but repeatably solvable
question. For $`k=0,\ldots,8`$ correct rollouts, this target gives the
QA reward vector $`(0,.5,1,.833,.667,.5,.333,.167,0)`$.

Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.1 Does the QA Agent Learn an Adaptive Curriculum? ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
compares both targets after the same $`50`$-step co-training budget. The
lower target obtains an unweighted overall score of $`49.1\%`$, $`3.3`$
points below the $`52.4\%`$ obtained by $`\tau=0.5`$. For multi-tool
deep search, difficult but reliably solvable questions are more useful
than questions that are merely close to failure. With $`K=8`$, a $`2/8`$
target has only one lower-success outcome before a question becomes
completely unsolved ($`k=0`$) and is discarded from the Solver update.
In contrast, a $`4/8`$ target keeps a wider margin of mixed-success
groups and supplies both successful and unsuccessful rollouts for
relative learning.

### 5.3 Does Updating the QA Policy Improve the Solver?

The cross-play evidence above measures whether a QA policy remains
informative as its Solver changes.
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.1 Does the QA Agent Learn an Adaptive Curriculum? ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
provides the outcome-level complement: how much does a valid but fixed
QA policy improve the Solver, and what does updating that policy add?
The untuned Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct agent begins at $`35.87\%`$ average
accuracy under the same agent workflow. Holding the QA policy fixed
while retaining the online harness raises this score to $`44.28\%`$
($`+8.41`$ points). The frozen and adaptive runs start from the same
Solver initialization and use exactly the same seed contexts, harness,
tools, rollout budget, and training schedule; the only training
difference is whether the QA policy is updated. Thus, the initial frozen
QA policy and harness are already useful—they generate verified
questions that train the Solver beyond its base capability. Updating the
QA policy throughout training raises the average further to $`52.40\%`$,
an additional $`+8.12`$ points over the frozen-QA control and $`+16.53`$
points over the base Solver. This pattern agrees with the checkpoint
cross-play: online QA construction alone helps, but a policy that
continues to adapt to Solver outcomes supplies a substantially stronger
curriculum.

### 5.4 Scaling to a Larger, Newer Backbone

Our gains are not confined to the $`8`$B setting. We also initialize
both policies from Qwen3.6-27B ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib38)), a larger
and newer backbone than the Qwen3-VL-8B Solver used in our main
experiments. On the same seed VQA contexts, the resulting MTA-Zero
raises the overall OOD accuracy from $`46.88\%`$ for its Qwen3.6-27B
base model to $`57.70\%`$ ($`+10.82`$ points;
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.1 Does the QA Agent Learn an Adaptive Curriculum? ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")).
The improvement is positive on every constituent benchmark: $`+2.3`$ on
MMSrch-Plus, $`+11.1`$ on HR-MMSrch, $`+7.5`$ on BC-VL, and $`+22.4`$ on
MMSrch. Thus, the online QA–Solver loop continues to improve a
substantially stronger Solver, rather than being specific to small
models.

Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.1 Does the QA Agent Learn an Adaptive Curriculum? ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
additionally provides context from reported 27–32B multimodal
deep-search agents. The external rows use earlier Qwen3-VL backbones,
including dense 32B and 30B-A3B MoE variants, whereas our matched
experiment uses Qwen3.6-27B. These values are not a controlled ranking:
benchmark subsets, tool stacks, search budgets, and judges differ across
papers. We therefore omit their aggregate scores and make the scaling
claim only from the local, matched base-versus-MTA-Zero comparison.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced MTA-Zero, an online QA–Solver co-training framework for
improving multimodal deep-search agents without a pre-generated
multi-hop corpus or an additional task-specific SFT stage. A trainable
QA Generator retrieves evidence and builds multi-hop questions. The
Solver’s group rollout outcomes then update both policies with separate
GRPO objectives: the QA Generator learns to propose questions that are
difficult but solvable for the current Solver, while the Solver learns
from the resulting mixed-outcome groups. Across six multimodal
deep-search evaluation benchmarks, MTA-Zero improves a Qwen3-VL-$`8`$B
Solver from $`36.91\%`$ to $`51.58\%`$ mean accuracy under the same
agent workflow, while also improving a newer Qwen3.6-$`27`$B backbone.
The experiments show that a valid static QA policy becomes increasingly
mismatched as the Solver changes, whereas updating the QA policy
restores a larger supply of useful training groups. The reward ablation
further shows that questions should be challenging without being pushed
too close to universal failure. These results support verified online
task generation as a practical route to self-improving multimodal
deep-search agents. Extending the harness to richer tool environments
while reducing multi-tool rollout cost is a promising direction for
future work.

### AI Use Statement

We used generative AI tools for literature organization, plotting and
analysis code, and experiment-orchestration and debugging scripts. The
research questions, method design, interpretation, and conclusions are
the authors’ own; the authors reviewed and tested AI-assisted code and
verified reported results against experiment outputs and raw logs.
Generative models also have substantive roles in the method and
evaluation: Qwen models instantiate the trainable QA Generator and
Solver, a frozen Claude Sonnet $`5`$ endpoint supports model-assisted
harness checks, gpt-5-mini adjudicates answers not resolved by
deterministic matching, and Claude $`4.8`$ Opus is used for the external
QA-quality audit. Proprietary models are additionally evaluated as
baselines. These uses are described in the corresponding method,
experiment, and appendix sections. We take responsibility for the final
text, claims, code, and experimental artifacts reported in this work.

### Ethics Statement

This work uses publicly released models and VQA datasets together with
publicly accessible web search results. The reported manual audit
evaluates model outputs rather than participant behavior or personal
attributes. We do not intentionally target private or sensitive
information, although live web retrieval can surface personal,
copyrighted, biased, outdated, or otherwise unreliable material. The
fixed harness and answer adjudication reduce but do not eliminate these
risks. Improved deep-search agents also carry dual-use risks by making
large-scale information collection and synthesis easier. Deployments in
high-stakes settings should therefore use appropriate access controls,
source review, and human oversight. We report the main run’s compute and
external-call footprint in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Online Data and Workload Accounting ‣ Appendix D Training and Evaluation Details ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").

### Reproducibility Statement

Sections [3](#S3 "3 Method ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
and [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Experiment Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
specify the model, data, tool-use protocol, rewards, and optimization
setup. The appendix provides the QA state and entity definitions,
ordered harness checks, Solver interfaces, token-level masking rules,
scoring procedure, training configuration, and verified workload and
resource accounting. Training uses publicly released Qwen backbones and
seed contexts drawn from public VQA datasets. Exact replay of live
retrieval and proprietary model-assisted checks may vary with web
content and service versions; we therefore separate deterministic checks
from model-assisted checks and report their roles and failure behavior.
These disclosures support protocol-level reproduction while making the
remaining dependency on time-varying external services explicit.

## Appendix A Detailed Agent Protocols

### A.1 Bridge-Entity Definition and Generator State

Following the entity convention used to construct our seed pool ([Peng
et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)), we define a *bridge entity* at every
non-final hop as a single proper-name answer that denotes one
unambiguous real-world referent, is supported by the retrieved evidence,
and can anchor the next retrieval step. This covers named referents from
the categories summarized in
Table [6](#A1.T6 "Table 6 ‣ A.1 Bridge-Entity Definition and Generator State ‣ Appendix A Detailed Agent Protocols ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").

|  Category |  Included referents |  Valid bridge-answer examples |
|----|----|----|
|  People |  Uniquely named public, historical, scientific, or athletic figures |  Ada Lovelace; Serena Williams |
|  Organizations |  Named institutions, companies, universities, government bodies, or sports teams |  UNESCO; FC Barcelona |
|  Locations and landmarks |  Specific geographic, natural, or architectural referents |  Nairobi; Machu Picchu |
|  Products |  Commercially named devices, vehicles, software, or other products |  PlayStation $`5`$; Toyota Prius |
|  Events |  Named sporting, historical, academic, or cultural events |  Cannes Film Festival; $`2016`$ Summer Olympics |
|  Creative works |  Titled films, books, artworks, television series, or music |  Spirited Away; The Starry Night |
|  Science and technology |  Named species, compounds, devices, models, or datasets |  Tyrannosaurus rex; BERT |
|  Medical and health |  Named diseases, conditions, or other specific medical entities |  Alzheimer’s disease; dengue fever |
|  Business and finance |  Named brands, firms, indexes, or financial instruments |  Patagonia; Nasdaq-$`100`$ |
|  Space and astronomy |  Named celestial objects, missions, telescopes, or astronomical events |  Voyager $`1`$; Andromeda Galaxy |

Table 6: Bridge-entity taxonomy used by the QA construction system,
adapted from the seed-selection convention of MTA-Agent ([Peng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib1)). The taxonomy constrains intermediate answers, which
must support another retrieval step; a final-hop answer may instead be a
short non-entity fact.

A multi-entity answer, unsupported alias, descriptive phrase, generic
category, action, or bare quantity is not a valid bridge entity. The
final hop need not support another extension: when the final-hop
quantity option is enabled, it may instead end in an exact count,
measurement, date, or other short factual answer.

The policy proposes the complete answer string $`a^{h}`$, but it does
not create the two entity representations used by the next turn. After
accepting a non-final hop, the fixed harness derives $`e^{h}`$, a short
canonical form used inside the next subquestion, and $`\tilde{e}^{h}`$,
a fully disambiguated form used inside the next search query. For
example, an accepted answer “Window Rock, Arizona” is represented as
$`e^{h}=`$ “Window Rock” and $`\tilde{e}^{h}=`$ “Window Rock, Arizona,
the capital of the Navajo Nation.” This separation keeps questions
readable while making retrieval queries unambiguous.

At hop $`h`$, the policy state contains the seed image, the running
merged question $`\bar{q}^{h}`$, $`e^{h}`$, $`\tilde{e}^{h}`$, the
accepted answer history, the latest harness observation, and the
remaining hop/turn budget. Its two actions and the corresponding
fixed-harness responses are summarized below.

|  Stage |  Trainable QA Generator output |  Fixed harness observation |
|----|----|----|
|  Search |  action, thought, tool=search, and query; the query must contain $`\tilde{e}^{h}`$. |  Retrieved and filtered evidence chunks, followed by a request to propose one supported next-hop QA pair. |
|  Proposal |  action, thought, question, answer, evidence, and source; the question must depend on $`e^{h}`$. |  Either an acceptance containing $`\bar{q}^{h+1}`$, $`e^{h+1}`$, and $`\tilde{e}^{h+1}`$, or a rejection diagnosis that preserves the last accepted state. |

Table 7: QA Generator state transitions. Harness observations are
appended as user turns and are always masked from the policy loss.

## Appendix B QA Harness Checks and Feedback

The QA harness is fixed throughout co-training. Its validation and
merging stages follow MTA-Agent ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)); our
adaptation exposes structured accept/reject feedback to the online QA
policy and masks rejected action spans. The harness uses retrieval
together with fixed programmatic and model-based checks, but its
parameters are not optimized and no gradient flows through it. The main
run uses Serper ¹¹ 1 [https://serper.dev/](https://serper.dev/) for text
retrieval and routes all model-assisted harness calls through the same
frozen Claude Sonnet $`5`$ endpoint on AWS Bedrock. Calls use a
$`60`$-second timeout and at most $`3`$ API attempts. The ordered checks
are detailed in
Table [8](#A2.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix B QA Harness Checks and Feedback ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").

| \# |  Stage |  Operation |  Failure behavior |
|----|----|----|----|
| $`1`$ |  Retrieve and filter |  Text search returns at most $`6`$ results. The filter may read up to $`6{,}000`$ characters per result and exposes at most $`6`$ evidence chunks of $`1{,}200`$ characters each to the QA policy; raw text retained internally is capped at $`8{,}000`$ characters per result. |  An empty/failed search rejects the attempt. If the filter call is unavailable or malformed, bounded raw snippets are used; an explicit empty filtered set rejects the attempt. |
| $`2`$ |  Structural and rarity gates |  Require nonempty question, answer, and evidence; reject a repeated answer or an answer appearing in more than $`3`$ retrieved chunks. |  Deterministic rejection. |
| $`3`$ |  Entity continuity |  Compare the proposed question against both the short current entity $`e^{h}`$ and its disambiguated form $`\tilde{e}^{h}`$, checking that the question truly depends on the same referent. |  A valid negative verdict rejects; an unavailable or malformed model verdict does not veto the proposal. |
| $`4`$ |  Proposal quality |  Rule-based and model-assisted checks test the proposal’s supplied evidence for support, and test uniqueness, temporal stability, entity necessity, stand-alone wording, and non-final answer linkability. |  Rule violations reject deterministically; an unavailable or malformed model verdict does not veto the proposal. |
| $`5`$ |  Merge and normalize |  Replace the previous explicit entity in the new question with the running description; return the merged question together with $`e^{h+1}`$ and $`\tilde{e}^{h+1}`$. |  Missing or unparsable merged output rejects the attempt. |
| $`6`$ |  Merged-QA coherence |  Check whether the merged question remains self-contained and has the proposed answer as its unique intended resolution. |  A valid negative verdict rejects; an unavailable or malformed verdict does not veto the proposal. |
| $`7`$ |  Parametric direct-answer gate |  Ask the frozen helper to answer the merged question without web access. The proposal is rejected when its expected answer appears in that response under case-insensitive substring matching. |  A failed helper call does not veto the proposal. |

Table 8: Fixed QA-harness execution order. Model-call failure behavior
is reported explicitly; verifier availability is monitored during
training.

For an accepted proposal, the harness appends a user-turn observation
containing $`\bar{q}^{h}`$, $`a^{h}`$, and an acceptance message. This
is the state used for the next Generator decision. A rejected proposal
instead produces diagnostic feedback, allowing another attempt while
preserving the previous accepted state. Both types of feedback remain
visible in the context. However, only the search action and QA proposal
associated with an accepted hop receive the QA policy-gradient signal.
Tokens from rejected attempts are masked from the QA loss.

### B.2 External Quality Audit of Generated QA Tasks

The rollout-success target alone does not guarantee that a QA Generator
avoids ambiguous or otherwise shortcut tasks. We therefore conduct an
external LLM-based quality audit with Claude $`4.8`$ Opus, separately
from the QA harness and Solver. For each of $`Q_{0}`$ and $`Q_{50}`$,
the audit assesses $`512`$ generated tasks under the same fixed rubric.
The evaluator inspects each final task and its recorded construction
trace, and returns a binary judgment for every criterion below.

| Audit criterion               | $`Q_{0}`$  | $`Q_{50}`$ |
|-------------------------------|------------|------------|
| Valid generated task          | $`90.0\%`$ | $`92.0\%`$ |
| Evidence / chain support      | $`70.3\%`$ | $`80.3\%`$ |
| Answer unique and stable      | $`81.3\%`$ | $`83.0\%`$ |
| Self-contained question       | $`90.2\%`$ | $`93.5\%`$ |
| No answer or evidence leakage | $`87.9\%`$ | $`89.8\%`$ |
| Requires the seed image       | $`73.8\%`$ | $`73.0\%`$ |

Table 9: External QA-quality audit of generated tasks. Claude $`4.8`$
Opus audits $`512`$ tasks from each QA checkpoint under the same fixed
rubric. Values are the percentage of tasks judged to satisfy each
criterion; higher is better.

##### Audit criteria.

*Valid generated task* requires a usable final question–answer pair.
*Evidence / chain support* requires that the cited evidence supports
each accepted hop and that the merged chain preserves the intended
answer. *Answer unique and stable* rejects plausible alternative answers
or time-sensitive answers without an explicit date. *Self-contained*
checks that the final question can be interpreted without the hidden
construction state. *No answer or evidence leakage* checks that
intermediate answers and minting evidence do not appear in the final
task. Finally, *requires the seed image* tests whether the image remains
necessary to answer the final question.

As
Table [9](#A2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ B.2 External Quality Audit of Generated QA Tasks ‣ Appendix B QA Harness Checks and Feedback ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
shows, all five structural quality checks increase from $`Q_{0}`$ to
$`Q_{50}`$: validity, evidence/chain support, answer uniqueness,
self-containedness, and anti-leakage. In particular, evidence/chain
support rises by $`10.0`$ percentage points and self-containedness by
$`3.3`$ points. Image dependence is nearly unchanged, at $`73.8\%`$ for
$`Q_{0}`$ and $`73.0\%`$ for $`Q_{50}`$. This audit does not rule out
every possible shortcut or establish that every mixed-outcome group
tests the intended reasoning capability. It does, however, find no
detectable quality degradation from QA training in the direct signatures
of ambiguity, unsupported chains, answer leakage, or image irrelevance.

### B.3 Learning Boundary of the Fixed Harness

The harness is a fixed task-construction environment, not a second
policy that generates the training questions. It contains retrieval
backends, programmatic filters, and fixed model-assisted checks, all
held unchanged throughout a run. In particular, it never selects the
next search action or its arguments, and it does not author the
candidate single-hop QA pair: these are outputs of the trainable QA
Generator.
Table [10](#A2.T10 "Table 10 ‣ B.3 Learning Boundary of the Fixed Harness ‣ Appendix B QA Harness Checks and Feedback ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training")
separates the responsibilities and learning signals.

|  Component |  Input $`\rightarrow`$ output |  Learning signal |
|----|----|----|
|  QA Generator |  State $`\rightarrow`$ tool and arguments, or proposed $`(q^{h},a^{h})`$ with evidence citation |  QA GRPO with scalar $`r_{i}^{\mathrm{Q}}`$ |
|  Fixed harness |  Tool request $`\rightarrow`$ bounded evidence; proposal $`\rightarrow`$ accept/reject feedback and merged question |  Fixed; no updated parameters, reward, or gradient |
|  Solver |  Seed image and final task $`\rightarrow`$ $`K`$ tool-use rollouts |  Solver GRPO with rollout correctness $`c_{ij}`$ |

Table 10: Learning boundary in the online QA construction loop.

##### Token-level QA credit assignment.

The harness may return filtered evidence, a diagnostic rejection, or a
merged question, but each is appended as an observation rather than a
target completion and is always masked from the QA loss. For an accepted
hop, the entire Generator-produced assistant span—reasoning, tool
selection, tool arguments, and the proposed question, answer, and
evidence citation—remains trainable. If the hop is rejected, the
corresponding span is masked starting from that attempt’s tool
selection; this masks its reasoning, arguments, and proposal together,
while keeping the content visible as context for the next attempt. A
later rejection never retroactively masks earlier accepted hops. If
generation stops before the target depth but has accepted earlier hops,
the current merged partial QA task is retained and those accepted spans
remain trainable.

##### Rewards and update order.

For each generated task, the $`K=8`$ binary Solver outcomes are first
reduced to $`p_{i}`$. With the main target $`\tau=0.5`$, the QA
Generator receives the single scalar Goldilocks reward

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{i}^{\mathrm{Q}}=\begin{cases}1-2\lvert p_{i}-0.5\rvert,&0<p_{i}<1,\\
0,&p_{i}\in\{0,1\}.\end{cases}
``` |  |

The $`N_{\mathrm{QA}}=8`$ candidate trajectories from one seed form one
QA GRPO group. Consequently, a candidate with reward zero is not
automatically dropped: it can receive a negative relative advantage when
other candidates from that seed have higher reward. The main $`8`$B run
keeps only Solver groups with $`0<p_{i}<1`$ and uses the individual
binary correctness values $`c_{ij}`$ as their terminal rewards; it
enables neither a function-call format gate nor hop-level partial
credit. Each iteration executes QA rollout, harness construction, $`K`$
Solver rollouts per task, correctness and QA-reward calculation, then
the QA update and the Solver update. Both updates therefore use the same
pre-update rollout batch; the QA update does not regenerate the Solver
data within that iteration.

##### Information isolation.

The Solver receives the seed image and final merged question, but not
the Generator’s intermediate QA pairs, their answers, minting evidence,
or mint source URLs. Answer-bearing mint URLs are recorded only as
blocked retrieval URLs. The image URL is used solely as a handle for
image tools such as reverse image search, OCR, and cropping; no source
HTML URL or other seed provenance metadata is provided to the Solver.
Thus, model-assisted checks can control task quality, but they do not
provide the Solver’s answer or share a trainable representation,
optimizer, or gradient with either policy. The QA Generator sees only
its harness feedback and the scalar $`r_{i}^{\mathrm{Q}}`$, never Solver
tokens, hidden states, or gradients. The two policies have separate
actor parameters and optimizers; the main run does not enable a
KL/reference-policy loss for either policy.

## Appendix C Solver Interaction and Tool Interfaces

For each Solver input, a rollout starts from its seed image and final
merged question. At every ReAct step, the Solver emits a reasoning
trace, an action, a should_stop decision, and a confidence score. An
action specifies a tool, its arguments, a short action description, and
the expected observation. The observation server executes the tool call
and appends the result to the interaction history before the next
decision. The rollout finishes when the Solver returns its final answer,
when should_stop is true with confidence above $`0.7`$, or when it
reaches the $`T=10`$-step budget. The final answer is emitted in a
designated boxed-answer field for evaluation.

For every question $`q_{i}`$, we sample $`K=8`$ complete rollouts. We
first apply answer normalization and matching, and use a fixed semantic
judge only for unresolved aliases or paraphrases. This yields the binary
terminal correctness $`c_{ij}`$ of rollout $`j`$. Its group rate
$`p_{i}`$ determines the Goldilocks score used by the QA Generator and
whether the Solver group is retained for GRPO. Tool observations are
part of the rollout context and are masked from the policy loss.

### C.1 Tool Palette

The Solver uses the following $`6`$ callable tools in the reported
multi-tool environment.

|  Tool |  Arguments |  Representative returned response |
|----|----|----|
|  Web search |  query |  Tool: web_search Response: The building was constructed to display and promote local products, commerce, and industry. |
|  Web image search |  query |  Tool: image_search Response: Search returned web image results about Payette Lake near McCall, Idaho. A geographic source identifies its outflow as the Payette River. |
|  Web-page reader |  url |  Tool: content_extraction URL: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parc_de_Belleville Response: Page topic: Parc de Belleville, an urban park in Paris. |
|  Reverse image search |  image_url; optional query |  Tool: reverse_image_search Response: The image most strongly matches the Petit Trianon at the Ch^ateau de Versailles. Visual matches include photos and pages associated with this landmark. |
|  OCR |  image_url |  Tool: ocr_tool Response: Text found in image: Sign: KOMORA WARSZAWA XIX W. THE WARSZAWA CHAMBER (19TH CENTURY) |
|  Image cropping |  image_url, crop_area |  Tool: image_cropping Output: Reasoning: Crop tightly around the central ruined dome-shaped building. Original size: $`(800,564)`$; Crops $`(1)`$: ruined dome building \| bbox=\[…\] \[cropped image attached\] |

Table 11: Solver tool-call interfaces and representative responses
appended to the next Solver turn. The first five response excerpts are
from recorded validation trajectories. The cropping response is from a

## Appendix D Training and Evaluation Details

### D.1 Seed-Pool Construction

We select the one-hop starting contexts using the seed-filtering
protocol of MTA-Agent ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)). A source item
must have an image-dependent question, a visually correct answer, and a
single specific answer entity. We discard the previously generated
extensions, evidence, and tool trajectory and retain only
$`(I,q^{1},a^{1})`$.

The fixed pool contains $`1{,}019`$ contexts: $`398`$ from InfoSeek,
$`300`$ from FVQA-train, $`190`$ from InfoVQA, and $`131`$ from OK-VQA.
Although the source records also store a disambiguated answer field, the
online data loader passes only $`I`$, $`q^{1}`$, and $`a^{1}`$ to the QA
Generator; no source chain or answer metadata is used. Consequently, the
comparison to MTA-Agent starts from its filtered one-hop contexts while
requiring MTA-Zero to construct every training-time multi-hop task
online.

### D.2 Main Co-training Configuration

Both policies begin from separate copies of Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. The
fixed seed pool combines the four public one-hop VQA sources listed in
Section [4.1.1](#S4.SS1.SSS1 "4.1.1 Datasets ‣ 4.1 Experiment Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA–Solver Co-training").
Each seed supplies an image and one question–answer pair. It contains
neither multi-hop questions nor retrieved evidence. The following
configuration is used for the main $`8`$B co-training run.

| Setting | Value |
|----|----|
| Seed contexts per iteration | $`8`$ |
| QA trajectories per seed | $`N_{\mathrm{QA}}=8`$ |
| Target construction depth | $`5`$ hops ($`1`$ seed + $`4`$ extensions) |
| Solver rollouts per QA input | $`K=8`$ |
| Configured QA / Solver max_turns | $`16`$ / $`10`$ |
| Search attempts / hop | $`3`$ |
| Prompt / response token limits | $`8{,}192`$ / $`24{,}576`$ |
| Co-training iterations | $`50`$ |
| Learning rate | $`10^{-6}`$ |
| QA sampling temperature / top-$`p`$ | $`1.0`$ / $`0.95`$ |
| Default QA target | $`\tau=0.5`$ |

Table 12: Main $`8`$B co-training configuration.

Each iteration therefore contains $`8\times 8=64`$ QA-generation
trajectories and schedules $`8\times 8\times 8=512`$ Solver rollout
inputs. The QA Generator and Solver use separate parameters, optimizers,
and GRPO updates; the main run does not enable a KL/reference-policy
loss. The only Solver-to-Generator signal is the scalar rollout-derived
score; no trajectory, hidden state, or gradient is shared between the
two policies.

### D.4 Answer Scoring and LLM Adjudication

We evaluate the final Solver using the same ReAct interaction protocol
as at training time and report accuracy. For each benchmark item, we
extract the final boxed answer when present (otherwise the final
response text) and first apply a deterministic, normalized match against
the set of acceptable reference answers. This rule stage handles
differences such as capitalization, whitespace, and standard
multiple-choice formatting.

Only when this match fails do we invoke the semantic judge, gpt-5-mini.
The judge receives the research question, all accepted reference
answers, and the model’s extracted final answer. It is instructed to
decide whether the candidate conveys the same core information as a
reference, allowing harmless aliases, paraphrases, and formatting
variation, and returns a JSON verdict with a Boolean correctness field
and a brief reason. A response is counted as correct if either the rule
stage or the semantic judge returns a positive verdict.

##### Human audit.

To assess the reliability of LLM adjudication, we manually re-evaluated
$`100`$ LLM-judged answers and found $`98\%`$ agreement between the
semantic judge and human correctness labels.
````
